sec.title: Background
sec.p: The effect of anesthesia methods on non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) recurrence post-resection remains uncertain. We aimed to compare the oncological outcomes of spinal anesthesia (SA) and general anesthesia (GA) in patients with NMIBC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This prospective randomized controlled trial recruited 287 patients with clinical NMIBC at Seoul National University Hospital from 2018 to 2020. The patients underwent transurethral resection of the bladder tumor within 4 weeks of randomization. Intrathecal hyperbaric bupivacaine (0.5%) and a mixture of propofol (1–2 mg/kg) and fentanyl (50–100 μg/kg) were used as induction agents in the SA and GA groups, respectively, with desflurane or sevoflurane used for maintaining anesthesia. The primary and secondary outcome measures were disease recurrence and disease progression, respectively, at 2 years after resection. Cumulative incidence of outcomes was compared between the two groups using time-to-event analyses.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 15 patients required alternative anesthesia owing to clinical needs such as SA failure or significant obturator reflex, resulting in a modified intention-to-treat (ITT) population of 272 patients. Time-to-event analysis showed a significantly lower recurrence of NMIBC in the SA group than in the GA group, in both ITT (27.4% vs 39.8%) and modified ITT populations (26.8% vs 39.6%). Disease progression occurred more frequently in the GA than in the SA group (15.2% vs 7.8%), although the difference was not statistically significant.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: A notable reduction in the 2-year recurrence rate was observed in patients who underwent SA than in those who underwent GA. Thus, SA may be considered the preferred anesthetic approach.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) recurrence rate is too high. We need to know if anesthesia methods affect the tumor recurrence of NMIBC.

For patients with NMIBC undergoing transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT), spinal anesthesia (SA) was associated with a decreased 2-year recurrence rate compared with general anesthesia in this randomized clinical trial.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: The choice of anesthesia approach may impact the oncological outcome for patients with NMIBC undergoing TURBT. To reduce the risk of disease recurrence, urologists and anesthesiologists should preoperatively consider SA.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Bladder cancer is ranked as the 10th most diagnosed cancer globally in 20201 and has emerged as a major public health concern. Its escalating incidence, coupled with having the highest lifetime treatment cost among all cancers,2 underscores its substantial impact on both individuals’ lives and healthcare economies. Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) accounts for approximately 75% of newly diagnosed bladder cancers.3 The primary management modalities for NMIBC involve transurethral resection and intravesical therapy.4 However, the considerable recurrence rate (31%–78%) and progression rate (15%) associated with NMIBC pose substantial challenges to enhancing patient quality of life and overall survival (OS).5

Recent advancements in cancer treatment have highlighted the significance of immunomodulation, particularly in the context of immune-hot tumors such as cancers of the bladder, which are characterized by high levels of immune cell infiltration and immune checkpoint molecules and are thus more responsive to immunotherapy.6 Despite these advances, the therapeutic impact of immune checkpoint inhibitors in NMIBC remains limited compared with that in MIBC,7 possibly because of diverse immunomodulatory perioperative factors.8 Efforts have been made to elucidate the influence of perioperative factors on oncological outcomes, with various retrospective studies exploring the role of anesthetic methods.912 However, the lack of consensus due to conflicting results has hindered the establishment of robust evidence in this domain.

In response to this unresolved question, we designed a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to systematically compare the oncological outcomes of spinal anesthesia (SA) and general anesthesia (GA) in patients with NMIBC. Based on previous reports suggesting that regional anesthesia (RA) may theoretically be superior to GA in preserving tumor-inhibitory immune function,13 14 we hypothesized that SA might be more effective in suppressing bladder cancer recurrence in patients with NMIBC undergoing transurethral resection of bladder tumors (TURBT). Here, we present 2-year tumor recurrence rates after resection under SA or GA, aiming to contribute to the ongoing discourse surrounding the impact of anesthetic methods on NMIBC outcomes.

sec.title: Trial design and participants
sec.p: This single-center, prospective RCT was conducted at Seoul National University Hospital in the Republic of Korea. Patients aged ≥18 years who were diagnosed with clinical NMIBC (Ta/T1) and capable of undergoing both SA and GA met the inclusion criteria. The exclusion criteria were concomitant upper tract urothelial carcinoma, ongoing treatment for other cancers, clinical suspicion of MIBC, immunological disease, current immunosuppressive therapy, or refusal to participate. Patient randomization was required within 4 weeks of diagnosis.

The study was conducted in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations, good clinical practice, and ethical principles as described in the Declaration of Helsinki. The results are reported in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials statement. The study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT03597087; Date of registration: July 2, 2018). URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03597087). The first patient was enrolled on July 27, 2018. The study ran from July 27, 2018 to April 13, 2022.

sec.title: Randomization
sec.p: A computer-generated, randomly permuted block design (https://www.sealedenvelope.com/) with varying block sizes was used to develop a 1:1 random allocation list for each stratum (SA and GA). The allocation sequence, generated by a person not involved in the enrolment or future data collection and analysis, was concealed using opaque, sealed, and sequentially numbered envelopes. The envelopes were opened only after the participants’ names were written on them to ensure allocation concealment. Screening and randomization were performed during TURBT planning in outpatient clinics.

sec.title: Intervention
sec.p: All enrolled patients underwent TURBT within 4 weeks of randomization. Standard monitoring was conducted in the operating room. Patients in the SA group received intrathecal hyperbaric bupivacaine (0.5%) via lumbar puncture using a 25-gage Quincke bevel spinal needle (Tae Chang Industrial, Daegu, Korea) at the L3/4, L4/5, or L5/S1 interspace, while in the lateral decubitus position. The intrathecal dose of bupivacaine was determined at the discretion of the anesthesiologist. If the patient requested sedation, midazolam (1–5 mg/kg) was administered. Fentanyl (50–100 μg/kg) was also administered if the patient reported severe pain (Numeric Rating Scale score of 6 or higher). The GA group received a mixture of propofol (1–2 mg/kg) and fentanyl (50–100 μg/kg) as induction agents, with desflurane (6–8 vol%) or sevoflurane (2–3 vol%) used for maintaining anesthesia.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Study data were collected online using the Research Electronic Data Capture program15 at the Department of Urology at Seoul National University Hospital. Patient demographics, baseline laboratory findings, urine cytology, cystoscopy, CT findings, and perioperative details were recorded. During the 2-year follow-up period, patients visited every 3 months for urine cytology, cystoscopy, and annual CT to assess cancer recurrence and progression. American Urological Association (AUA) risk stratification data were collected according to a previous study.4

sec.title: Primary and secondary study outcomes
sec.p: The primary and secondary outcome measures were the 2-year recurrence and progression rates, respectively. Recurrence and progression rates were based on the pathological tissue examination results. Disease progression included both T-stage and tumor progression. Post hoc subgroup analysis was performed as a function of AUA risk group, age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking, Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) instillation, and re-TURBT.

sec.title: Sample size estimation
sec.p: In a referenced retrospective study comparing the recurrence rates between SA and GA in patients with NMIBC undergoing TURBT,10 the HR for GA compared with that for SA was 1.57, with a 2-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) rate of approximately 40% in the GA group. Based on this evidence, we assumed a 2-year RFS rate of 0.4 for the GA group and 0.56 for the SA group in our study. With an accrual time of 1 year and a follow-up time of 2 years, the required sample size to maintain a power of 0.8 at a significance level of 0.5 was 260 participants. Considering a 10% drop-out rate, we planned to enroll 287 participants (143 in the SA group and 144 in the GA group) in the clinical trial.

sec.title: Outcome analysis
sec.p: The efficacy outcomes were assessed in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population, which included all participants who underwent randomization, and in the modified ITT population, which included all participants who underwent randomization and received the appropriate type of anesthesia. Statistical comparisons were performed using the χ2 test (for categorical variables) and t-test (for continuous variables), with significance set at p<0.05. Group differences in primary and secondary outcomes over the 2-year follow-up were assessed using Kaplan-Meier plots and compared using the log-rank test. In the stratified subgroup analysis (post hoc analysis), Cox proportional hazards regression was used to estimate HR and 95% CIs to examine the relationship between the AUA risk group, age, sex, BMI, smoking, BCG instillation, re-TURBT, and risk of bladder cancer recurrence. HRs were not adjusted for this analysis. All p-values were two-sided, with a type I error (α=0.05) used to determine statistical significance. Analyses were performed using the SPSS software package (V.29.0; IBM SPSS), and a forest plot was created using GraphPad Prism V.10.0 (GraphPad Software, USA).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between August 2018 and April 2020, 287 patients were randomly assigned to undergo SA (143) or GA (144). Throughout the trial, 15 patients received an alternative anesthetic approach due to clinical needs such as SA failure and obturator reflex. This resulted in 272 patients with a modified ITT population (figure 1). The clinical characteristics were well balanced between the SA and GA groups, except for male predominance in the SA group (tables1 2). Both groups had similar ASA risk, T-stage, tumor grade, and anesthesia and operation durations. Since the inclusion criterion of this study was clinical NMIBC, there were cases in which the final pathological results revealed pathologies other than clinical NMIBC. These included MIBC, non-urothelial cancer, and benign pathologies, with no significant differences in their proportions between the two groups.

sec.p: For both SA and GA groups, no significant difference was observed in anesthesia (33.0±12.9 min vs 36.1±18.6 min) and operation durations (16.2±12.7 min vs 18.3±15.6 min; tables1 2). In the SA group, intrathecal bupivacaine (13.6±1.7 mg) was administered, and sensory loss was achieved between the T2 and T10 levels. Midazolam (2.5±1.3 mg) was administered to 17 patients. Fentanyl (100 μg/kg) was administered to one patient. In the GA group, desflurane and sevoflurane were used in 122 (85.9 %) and 20 (14.1%) patients, respectively. For induction, propofol (1.5±0.5 mg/kg) and fentanyl (74±29 μg/kg) were administered.

38 patients in the SA and 55 patients in the GA groups, respectively, showed disease recurrence, whereas 11 and 21 patients in the SA and GA groups, respectively, showed disease progression. Time-to-event analysis showed a significantly lower recurrence in the SA group than in the GA group in both the ITT (27.4% vs 39.8%, p=0.02; figure 2) and modified ITT populations (26.8% vs 39.6%, p=0.024; figure 3; primary outcome). Disease progression occurred more frequently in the GA group (15.2% vs 7.8%, p=0.056), although the difference was not statistically significant (figure 2).

sec.p: As post hoc analysis, the overall recurrence benefit across key subgroups is shown in online supplemental figure 1. The sample size and number of recurrences in some subgroups were small and the CIs were wide. The overall recurrence benefit by SA was pronounced in patients who had AUA high-risk (recurrence rate at 2 years, 27.5% (14 events) in the SA group vs 50.8% (30 events) in the GA group; HR for recurrence, 0.37, 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.67), but not in patients with AUA low risk/intermediate risk (recurrence rate at 2 years, 30.0% (15 events) in the SA group vs 25.5% (14 events) in the GA group; HR for recurrence, 1.18, 95% CI, 0.57 to 2.44). Time-to-event analysis also showed a significantly lower recurrence in the SA group than in the GA group in the AUA high-risk group (27.5% vs 53.5%, log-rank p<0.001). In contrast, no benefit was observed in the AUA low-to intermediate-risk group (30.0% vs 25.9%, log-rank p=0.660; online supplemental figure 2). Notable disease recurrence risk reduction was observed in the SA group than in the GA group in male patients (27.0% (31 events) in the SA group vs 38.9% (44 events) in the GA group; HR for recurrence, 0.62, 95% CI, 0.39 to 0.98), and older age (≥65) patient group (23.1% (18 events) in the SA group vs 40.5% (32 events) in the GA group; HR for recurrence, 0.49, 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.87).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The immunosuppressive effects of surgical stress, perioperative pain, and GA on the immune system are well established. They are mediated either directly or through activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis and the sympathetic nervous system.1618 In the context of NMIBC, our RCT revealed a significant reduction in the 2-year recurrence rate with SA compared with that with GA. This notable difference suggests a potential role of SA in preserving perioperative immune function, thereby influencing the oncological outcomes of NMIBC. In the post hoc analysis, observed benefits of SA were particularly pronounced in high-risk groups, aligning with the prolonged efficacy of intravesical BCG immunotherapy, which is a standard treatment for NMIBC.19 In contrast, no clear effect was observed in the low-risk and intermediate-risk groups. Ultimately, the significant results in the overall population reflect the strong risk reduction observed in the high-risk group. While the secondary outcome, progression rates, was not significantly different between the two anesthesia approaches, a discernible trend favoring SA was observed. We posit that a larger sample size and greater number of events may reveal a statistically significant impact of SA on PFS.

Li et al recently conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs investigating the effect of RA on the survival outcomes of various cancer types.2022 Their analysis included 15 RCTs that primarily focused on breast, colon, lung, prostate, and bladder cancers and assessed the main outcomes such as RFS and OS. Overall, the authors concluded that there was no significant evidence to support the role of RA in improving RFS or OS. Notably, most comparisons in these studies involved the additive effects of RA, such as epidural anesthesia and paravertebral block (PVB), with GA compared with those of GA alone, which differs from our study design.

In a study by Sessler et al, RA was directly compared with GA using propofol and PVB as RA in breast cancer surgery.23 This large multicenter RCT found that RA via PVB and propofol did not reduce breast cancer recurrence following potentially curative surgery compared with RA associated with GA alone. However, in a post hoc analysis, Li et al demonstrated the potential benefits of RA in a subset of high-risk breast cancer patients, specifically those with ER-negative tumors.24 This finding aligns with our results, suggesting that individuals at high risk of recurrence may derive greater benefits from RA.

Bladder cancer is a promising candidate for investigating the impact of RA on oncological outcomes for the following reasons: the pelvic nature of the bladder allows the feasibility of SA; the TURBT procedure is relatively straightforward and brief, reducing the likelihood of various confounding factors; bladder cancer inherently exhibits a high recurrence rate; and the critical importance of the perioperative period is underscored by the proven efficacy of postoperative mitomycin C in preventing recurrence.25 Several studies have investigated the effect of RA on bladder cancer, and a recent meta-analysis of observational studies by Illias et al revealed a significant reduction in cancer recurrence associated with RA.12 Notably, Koumpan et al asserted that SA led to a lower recurrence rate following TURBT than that with GA.10

This study has several limitations. First, the lower recurrence rate observed in the SA group did not translate into a benefit to lower progression rate, although it showed a tendency toward progression risk reduction. This discrepancy may be attributed to the failure to achieve an adequate sample size and a low progression rate of only 11.1% among the 287 patients. Considering that 7.7% (11 events) and 14.6% (21 events) of the patients in the SA and GA groups, respectively, showed progression at the 2-year mark, obtaining a larger sample size could potentially lead to more meaningful conclusions. Second, because the subgroup was not predesigned, we recognize there may be statistical power limitations. Based on our results, we believe that further RCT focusing on high-risk NMIBC with adequate sample sizes is necessary in the future. Third, a single surgeon conducted this RCT at a single center, highlighting the need for future multicenter studies.

Despite these limitations, this study had several strengths. First, the existing meta-analyses have failed to provide definitive conclusions regarding the role of SA in NMIBC.12 As the first RCT to report a significant reduction in recurrence rates with SA compared with that with GA in patients with NMIBC, this study is a source of high-level evidence. Second, varying recurrence rates were investigated based on the anesthesia methods, highlighting the surgical perspective and the comprehensive adjustment of perioperative factors that influence oncological outcomes. Moreover, this study presents an approach for optimizing the efficacy of diverse immune checkpoint inhibitors in NMIBC, suggesting avenues for exploration in future clinical trials. Third, contrary to the general notion that the benefits of anesthesia methods are more pronounced in major surgeries with aggressive tumor,26 our study suggests that even in the context of a minor surgery such as TURBT, there may be significant oncological benefits associated with the choice of anesthesia method, especially in cancers with a high risk of recurrence. Fourth, the critical importance of risk stratification in NMIBC was underscored. Specifically, the necessity for meticulous consideration in selecting anesthesia methods for patients at high risk of recurrence emphasizes the need for carefully crafted management plans tailored to the level of risk, which surgeons may easily overlook. Further exploration with larger sample sizes and mechanistic studies could offer deeper insights into the intricate interplay among anesthesia, immune function, and oncological outcomes in NMIBC.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this prospective randomized controlled TURBT, SA was associated with a decreased 2-year recurrence rate in patients than with GA. SA should be considered an anesthetic approach, especially for those who are at a high risk of disease recurrence.
